content: Gestational choriocarcinoma is a malignant tumor that originates from trophoblastic tissue associated with any gestational event during pregnancy in women of reproductive age. This tumor arises from abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic cells, which are cells that normally form part of the placenta. Women with gestational choriocarcinoma often present with abnormal vaginal bleeding, which may be persistent and unexplained. They may also exhibit persistently and markedly elevated levels of beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), a hormone typically associated with pregnancy. Additionally, a history of a prior pregnancy, including normal pregnancies, molar pregnancies, or miscarriages, is often noted in affected individuals. The majority of cases of gestational choriocarcinoma develop shortly after a gestational abnormality, such as a molar pregnancy or miscarriage. However, in some instances, the disease may manifest after a prolonged latency period, even years after the initial gestational event. On gross examination, the tumor typically appears as a red, hemorrhagic mass within the uterus. The size of the mass can vary significantly. Diagnosis is often presumptive and relies on clinical findings, including the identification of a malignant trophoblastic tumor, as well as laboratory and imaging studies. At the time of diagnosis, over 90% of patients already have metastases to the lungs. Less commonly, metastases may also be present in the brain and liver. Despite the advanced stage of disease at presentation, treatment with chemotherapy is highly effective, with an 80% five-year survival rate. However, in cases where the disease proves fatal, death is typically due to complications arising from metastases to the liver and brain.
